The tunes of Seán Ryan ~

"The Hidden Ireland:
The First Selection of Irish Traditional Compositions of Seán Ryan"
Compiled by Brian Ryan

Page 10: “The Nightingale”

From the book:

“Seán Ryan was born in Nenagh, Co. Tipperary. It was his good fortune to grow up in the Newtown area, an environment steeped in Irish traditional music. The flute was his first instrument, but he began learning the fiddle at an early age. His father Thomas also was an outstanding fiddler. Seán was imbued with a great love for Ireland, her music, song, dance, culture, language, her people and games. He was a champion step-dancer and a very fine singer. ~ ” ~ Caitlín & Brian Ryan

It’s easy to confuse the two Sean Ryans at first. The whistle Sean Ryan lives in Tipperary, and that’s where fiddle Sean Ryan was from as well. Then we have the two box players named Paddy O’Brien of course. There’s also two Seamus Egans that both play banjo. Oh the humanity!

Re: The Nightingale

Hi

I’m new to the Session, so a bit late to the discussion.

I learned this tune in 1975 when I was hanging in Sligo with the band Pumpkinhead. They got it from the Sligo town fiddler Joe O‘Dowd, who often said, “Oh, don’t ask me now” when he couldn’t recall the name of a tune. They recorded it as part of a jig set as “Joe O’Dowd’s” on their 1976 LP on Mulligan. Kevin Burke played fiddle on the record.

https://irishrock.org/irodb/bands/pumpkinhead.html

I recorded it myself a few years later, also with Kevin Burke on fiddle, on a Kicking Mule LP called “After the Morning.” Kevin couldn’t recall the name of the tune at the time, either, so we also went with calling it after Joe O’Dowd.

Nice to finally learn the more common other names for it.

I’ll post the setting I know once I figure out how to do that.

Cheers!

↳ Posted by Mark-o on March 19th, 2019.

Re: The Nightingale

Tune’s title The Nightingale was christened by Fr John Quinn for Ryan and Quinn says: “I never heard a nightingale but I am told it has a beautiful song, and so gave this beautiful and such a traditionally sounding jig this name.” Quinn adds that Ryan won the 1960 newly composed tunes in the All Ireland with this tune together with “The Glen of Aherlow”(reel) and “The Wonder”(hornpipe).

↳ Posted by ConorW on August 26th, 2023.

Re: The Nightingale

The nightingale is essentially an African bird.
From May until the breeding season is over, it leaves the northern subtropical parts of Africa to nest in continental Europe; West from Morocco to Southern England and East from Poland to the Altai. It is absent from Scandinavia, Scotland and Ireland, but has long been celebrated everywhere in Europe, as part of a long tradition of courtly love songs and poetry. It is a symbol of courting and as an allegorical figure is known from Afghanistan to the Alleghenies. Its name appears in many traditional songs. In Irish, it is known as fílimeala, which is one of several names Ovid gave him (philo+melos). Like the young lovers obliged to go night-visiting (think Romeo & Juliet) he will croon and warble long into the night (hence ‘night’ingale).
The bulbul variety (1 of 3 subspecies) is the national bird of Iran; its name is onomatopeic and every second Persian song alludes to it, it seems!

Its favorite habitat is willow scrubland. And although there is plenty of that around Tipperary (of all places, Ros Fhionnghlaise, meaning ‘wood of the clear stream’, is just the kind of location two nightingale hopefuls would want to establish their homestead in!) there is little chance Fr. John Quinn or Seán Ryan would have heard one in their days.
Many birds long unknown in Ireland, such as the white egret or the woodpecker, are now settling here, pushed and pulled by various factors into finding new territories. Who knows: the days of the Irish nightingale might be only a couple of springs ahead now? Keep an ear out for the male’s sharp burbling song this May!
